problem: "So Cp is always larger than Cv" is too strong and contradicts Q4 of this chapter. When α = 0 the two are equal — water at about 4 °C is the standard example — so the difference is never negative but can be zero.
fix: Write: "So Cp ≥ Cv, with equality when α = 0 (water near 4 °C)."

problem: "Cp − Cv is the extra heat a substance needs" misses the per-kelvin part; the difference of two heat capacities is extra heat per unit temperature rise, not extra heat.
fix: "Cp − Cv is the extra heat per kelvin a substance needs at constant pressure, because it also expands."

problem: The lead says the same PVT derivatives (α and κ_T) give how Cp and Cv change with pressure and volume. Those slopes come from second derivatives of v or P, not from α and κ_T themselves, so the sentence misleads a student into expecting α and κ_T to be enough.
fix: "Second derivatives of the equation of state give how Cp changes with pressure and Cv with volume, and hence the ratio γ = Cp/Cv."

problem: Both inputs from the α, κ_T node are labelled "divide", but in Tvα²/κ_T the coefficient α is squared and multiplied; only κ_T is divided.
fix: Split the edge labels: "square, multiply" from α and "divide" from κ_T, or label the node edge as "α² multiply, κ_T divide".

problem: The Gibbs-Helmholtz sentence appears with no link to Cp or Cv and is not used again; a student cannot see why it is here.
fix: Either drop it, or add one line: it gives how H/T varies with temperature at fixed P, and combining it with Cp = (∂H/∂T)_P shows how enthalpy and Cp are tied together.
